The thesis introduces an integer linear programming model to address the scheduling problem of the National Hockey League's regular season. This approach formalizes the scheduling task as a discrete optimization problem, where binary variables represent game assignments and constraints enforce fairness, economic viability, and logistical requirements. The mathematical formulation enables systematic exploration of feasible solutions but faces a fundamental computational barrier—exponential complexity—preventing resolution of realistic-sized instances. Dualities emerge between theoretical optimality and practical implementability, revealing that while the model provides a rigorous foundation, it fails to scale without heuristic augmentation or approximation techniques. The derivation highlights how mathematical abstraction can capture real-world complexities yet remains constrained by algorithmic limitations inherent in combinatorial optimization.
